The paper includes useful ablations and diagnostics, including encoder/decoder balance, query initialization, complementary masking, distillation compatibility, training throughput, longer-context inference throughput, precision effects, and sampling variants.
The method appears practically interesting because it is compatible with masked-model sampling and distillation, and the appendix gives a reasonable amount of implementation and compute detail.
weaknesses: The strongest OpenWebText quality results rely on larger PGM models than the MDLM baseline, and the parameter-matched PGM setting appears weaker or incompletely reported at full training. This makes the quality-efficiency tradeoff less clean than the headline suggests.

The likelihood/perplexity interpretation for PGM is not fully justified. Since PGM changes the conditioning structure and predicts both partitions from each other, the paper should more rigorously derive the training objective, likelihood bound, and downstream scoring procedure.

Language generation evaluation is somewhat limited. Generative perplexity with GPT-2 Large and unigram entropy are useful but insufficient; only 1024 samples are used, no qualitative samples or human/LLM-based evaluation are shown, and downstream task accuracies are low and only modestly different.

The comparison set is narrow. For language, the main baseline is MDLM, with no direct experimental comparison to recent hybrid or efficient masked/diffusion approaches such as Block Diffusion or Eso-LMs, nor a careful speed-quality comparison against autoregressive models beyond a plot reference.

The speed claims are compelling but depend on implementation details, batch size, sequence length, sampler, and number of steps. More hardware-normalized analysis and optimized-baseline comparisons would make the inference advantage more definitive.

Some architectural details need sharper formalization, especially the exact attention masks needed to prevent information leakage and whether the implementation enforces the claimed conditional independence in all layers.

Reproducibility is decent but not complete: code and model artifacts are promised rather than available, and some experimental choices such as validation splits, sampler tuning, guidance selection, and precision choices could affect the reported numbers.

The strongest language results are not apples-to-apples: on OpenWebText, the same-size PGM underperforms MDLM, and the reported gains require larger models with more parameters. The downstream evaluation is questionable: using a variational bound on the full sequence as a substitute for continuation likelihood in lm-eval may introduce candidate-dependent bias, and the paper does not validate that this protocol is calibrated or comparable across models.

strengths: The paper targets a real bottleneck in masked generative models: full-length processing during sampling. The proposed partitioned formulation is a clear idea with an intuitive computational advantage.

The Partition Transformer architecture is reasonably well motivated: group-wise self-attention, a swap/cross-attention mechanism, and decoder-only prediction at queried positions together explain how the model can avoid processing mask tokens at inference.
The empirical evidence is broader than many borderline papers: language modeling, downstream language tasks, distillation compatibility, and ImageNet token generation are all evaluated.
The reported inference throughput gains are substantial, especially the 5x gains over MDLM on OpenWebText and the 7.5x batch-throughput gain over MaskGIT at comparable FID.
The paper includes useful ablations, including complementary masking, encoder/decoder balance, query initialization, sampling step counts, and additional appendix results.
weaknesses: The strongest text results are confounded by model size: the OpenWebText PGMs that beat MDLM use more layers or a larger hidden dimension, while same-size PGM results are weak or not fully reported at 1M steps.

The complementary masking baseline complicates the central claim: on LM1B, MDLM with complementary masking outperforms PGM, suggesting that part of the gain is due to denser supervision rather than the proposed architecture.

The language-generation evaluation is thin. Generative perplexity from GPT-2 Large plus unigram entropy and small downstream multiple-choice tasks are not enough to establish high-quality text generation, especially given known issues with Gen. PPL.

The objective and weighting discussion is confusing and may even have a group-label reversal: the paper should more rigorously justify why tokens in each partition receive w(t) versus w(1-t), and prove that the implementation matches the intended MGM objective.

The image results are promising but focus on throughput more than latency; single-sample latency gains appear much smaller than the headline 7.5x throughput number, so the claims should be worded more carefully.

Scalability is not established. Experiments are at relatively small language-model scale, context length above 1024 is only measured for inference without training, and training is currently slower due to dense attention masks.
Reproducibility is only partial: code and artifacts are promised for future release, several implementation details matter greatly, and some tables contain apparent formatting or numerical errors.
The paper has noticeable presentation issues, including typos, repeated words, inconsistent terminology, and table formatting problems, which undermine confidence but are not by themselves fatal.
